cards.title: Yes, and

depth.text: a professor says future programmers should still **write code**, even as **AI changes the job**

He says writing code helps juniors **learn to read it**, and recommends **AI as a TA** for getting past learning roadblocks instead of generating assignment code. He expects **software architecture** to become more important.

cards.camps: Two camps: fundamentals-first commenters say understanding code remains valuable; skeptics say AI may cut developer demand or make years spent learning to code a poor bet.

cards.title: ADHD as a circadian rhythm disorder: evidence and implications for chronotherapy (2025)

depth.text: the article links **body-clock shifts** with ADHD and says **changing sleep habits** may ease symptoms

The authors describe **delayed sleep timing** and shifted biological markers in a substantial subgroup, but not everyone. A child sleep program improved symptoms and functioning; the authors propose **routine sleep screening**, fixed wake times and morning bright light, with selective melatonin—not reclassifying ADHD exclusively as a circadian disorder.
data: ADHD patients with delayed sleep/wake cycle

cards.camps: Two camps: some see a strong, actionable sleep link; others say correlation doesn't make ADHD a circadian disorder, with early-riser counterexamples.

comments.text: Chronobiologist here. And also have ADHD. The associations with ADHD really are there, but that may just also be because a huge number of brain processes have a circadian regulation, and those get disrupted by whatever is causing ADHD. The causality is also bidirectional, because whatever ADHD does could cause light exposure behavioral changes, which could leave a circadian phenotype. In general…

> walk in > see this title > oh man that would explain a lot Ok after reading a chunk of this the correlation is pretty wild. Having the data it’s quite striking. Sleep intervention as a form of ADHD treatment has always seemed reasonable to me but this gives a lot more clarity to the approach and mechanisms. For me, the seasonal aspect of it aligns with their blue light findings (both driving…

Beware that Frontiers In is a very low quality outlet and most scientists stay far far away from it (unless they really need a publication the next three weeks since they have that tenure track review coming up). Eg see https://retractionwatch.com/2025/07/29/frontiers-retract-122...

Has anyone considered that one reason for being/staying awake late at night that's very salient for ADHD people is that night tends to be much quieter, so it's a period when it's much easier to think/read/work without constant interruptions. Noise pollution isn't taken seriously enough.

The title of the article is irresponsibly chosen. - My time in the field of psychology has made me think that the use of imprecise language for describing psychology has a large and problematic societal impact ADHD is correlated with but is NOT a "circadian rhythm disorder". This is definitionally true. There are many causes of ADHD. One of them is likely sleep issues.

cards.title: Ask HN: What do you run on a $5 VPS that's worth keeping online 24/7?

depth.text: people keep **small servers** running **photo libraries**, family tools, personal sites, and backups

Examples include **Immich** for personal photos and **Jellyfin** for media, plus family shopping lists, password stores, websites, and git backups. Some use a VPS as a **Yggdrasil** hub or VPN, while running heavier services at home.

cards.title: Orkut.com

depth.text: people miss **Orkut**, but some doubt its return can fix what went wrong with **social media**

David Jeske says he was Orkut’s technical architect and engineering director, and says it was **built in-house**. Orkut Büyükkökten wrote almost all of its first version in C# .NET as a 20% time project. Jeske says Brazil’s **country rankings** helped it spread; after the service was split by language, he says India saw a **second cultural explosion**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some would be interested if people could own their posts; others doubt a comeback can solve what’s wrong with social media.

comments.text: Orkut was HUGE. Google acquired it and it basically had *the* social media platform in Brazil pre-Facebook. IIRC, it also had a big-ish market share in some other countries. When Facebook came along, it was clear that Google was not doing as many updates as they needed to compete, so Orkut felt more and more "outdated". They killed it after a while to replace with "something better". That was…

Ah, a blast from the past! My wife and I met on Orkut in 2005. IIRC, there weren't any private messages for a long time, and it used to be a lot of fun reading everyone's messages to everyone else :-) :-) Used to be very large in India for quite a while.

I think we're past the social media era. I remember using facebook to connect with highschool friends and keep up with them when I was in college. We used to play barn buddy together, update status and used to chat for ages on fb chat. But everything got ruined when fb allowed re-posting and pages which allowed non-personal and unauthentic repetitive stuff to be on top of the feed instead of the…

Even if I cosign the spirit of the letter, this has big 90s viral email energy to the benefit of… another company/service/etc that I have no connection to. Sounds like his vision is to be a better version of Reddit. Could be good if done well. Not sure how doing his viral marketing for him plays into that. If I'm gonna send a friend a thing, I want it to be a thing I endorse.

In India, Orkut was a massive success back in the day. We've had testimonials, and we used to spend a lot of time writing them. We used to spend hours hacking the corporate firewall to access Orkut during office hours!

cards.title: US man given prison sentence for bot-farming music streams

depth.text: a US man got a **prison sentence** for using bots to **fake music streams**
One commenter says Smith used as many as **10,000 bot accounts** to stream music; others argue the fraud was **fake listening**, not making AI songs.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say fake streams were the fraud; others argue the case is unfair or inconsistently applied.

comments.text: I am not sure I understand. Surely a AI generated song isn't a "fake song"? Is it a crime to publish an AI generated song? It seems that what he is guilty of is to generate some fake users pretending to listen to his songs, is that right? I can see how it is fraud, but how is it different from all the dark patterns used by newspapers to generate more page prints (like auto-refreshing pages)?

Here’s what bothers me: isn’t the United States a free market? What crime did he actually commit? Using services exactly as they are offered? It turns out that now, if you take advantage of the system as it was designed and gain a financial edge, you become a criminal—but if a major corporation does it, they just get a slap on the wrist.

> At times SMITH was using as many as 10,000 Bot Accounts at once to fraudulently stream music, and he used fake email accounts and fraudulently-obtained debit cards to create the Bot Accounts I gather these are cards that he opened and funded, not stolen cards. I'm surprised at this scale it wasn't detected much sooner. These accounts had to be listening a lot in order to generate more royalties…

After talking at length with claude about this case it seems that while botting music streams does meet the bar for wire fraud, creating thousands of fake accounts on walmart to scalp pokemon cards does not. In my opinion these are the same thing, one just pays out from a shared royalty pool and the other on ebay. I guess that's a big difference from a legal perspective, but from a moral and…
If Spotify royalties were allocated fairly a scheme like this shouldn't be able to pull more money out than the subscriptions put in.

depth.text: someone made a **data lake format** where tables can be read and changed with **ordinary SQL**

The format is built on **SQL and Parquet**, with a **catalog database** holding metadata and Parquet files holding the data. One commenter says it doesn't require DuckDB and points to a **Rust/DataFusion initiative**.

comments.text: Don't think it's widely known or understood, but Ducklake doesn't require duckdb: it's just a (good) data lake spec that works in duckdb. There's a cool alternate rust/datafusion ecosystem initiative going on at https://github.com/datafusion-contrib/datafusion-ducklake , and think the Quack protocol opens up a lot of cool possibilities too. If you need an idea for what do do with ducklake…
Motherduck is offering a free copy of O'reilly's "DuckLake: The Definitive Guide" book on their DuckLake web page https://motherduck.com/product/ducklake/
But "Duckpond" was right there !

It's alright, it's pretty alpha software. On v1.5.4, catalog filtered counts are broken, afaik. I went to main/v2 to fix it, and then the SQL parser in duckdb v2 is 10x slower, which was another wrench in the gears. It's been a bit of a pain tbh

cards.title: Classic PC demoscene productions running natively in the browser

depth.text: someone got **classic PC demos** running in **your browser** by recreating the old hardware

An **x86 emulator** records each demo’s executed code, which is translated into C and compiled to **WebAssembly** with models of the timer, VGA card and Sound Blaster. The result is checked **event for event** against the emulator.

cards.camps: Two camps: critics say the port misses the point of a scene built on human skill; others welcome the nostalgia and marvel at how faithfully it runs.

comments.text: I understand that it might be nice to be able to play old demos in your browser, and its fine, but... Please keep AI away from the demoscene. Ive been active in the demoscene for almost 30 years, its a big part of my life, and i am truly worried people using AI to build tools and code demos will destroy it by removing the very reason why its interesting. I want to be impressed by real peoples…

> The demo is run on an x86 emulator that records every block of code the CPU actually executes, over the whole demo. > That recording is translated into C - the original instructions, one for one, with the exact cycle timing of the emulated machine. What's the advantage of this approach vs cycle-accurate emulation? (I'd guess it can go faster, due to compiler optimization?) > The result is…

The days I gave up with demoscene. When PC killed Atari ST and Amiga scene (sorry to put you after amiguys, but life was always easier for you ;) ), all the magic of fixed hardware without tons of Mhz and RAM, when we were running after that cathode ray which wouldn't wait, exploiting hardware bugs to break those damn borders above, below and sideways, spending hours turning my head upside-down…

Wow, this brings back memories! I got my first PC (a 486 DX2-66) in 1994 and got a Creative Soundblaster graphics card + speakers later that year. Second reality was the first demo I had on that PC. I remember being blown away by the graphics and audio... I showed it off to everyone. Of course it looks quite quaint now, but at the time I had just upgraded from a Commodore 64!

this is mind boggling! although during the 90s might have started to shift to use C in damascene production, but when I was most active (90-94) we were hand rolling a lot of code in assembly. memory "management" was pretty basic at best, code and data occasionally separated. maybe for demos it was less of thing, but for smaller intros, writing into the code during runtime was maybe not everyday…

cards.title: Show HN: Making a flexible "neon" t-shirt with LED filaments

depth.text: someone is making a flexible **neon T-shirt** with **LED filaments**
One commenter asks whether **LED filament** is the same as EL wire; another describes a costume filament that shocked them, then measured **240V** despite the two AA batteries.

comments.text: Yeah I do kinda the same but I embed them into latex prosthetics. Like horns or protrusions for the face that you glue on. They're really good for a cyberpunkey vibe. I'm just casting some at the moment actually because we're coming up on Halloween soon. They look great but they're difficult to solder. Too little heat and it doesn't attach, too much and it damages them. The strip has some…
Looks solid, best of luck with it.
Author here, happy to answer any questions!

One of my kids had something like this built into a Halloween costume that their mom procured from Amazon. One of the filaments was blinking out within a day so I started running the length of the filament to figure out where the bad connection was. Unexpectedly it shocked the hell out of me. I put a meter on it and it was 240V. I couldn't believe I got such a nasty poke from 2 AA batteries.
That's a nice wearable!

glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.TA: Teaching assistant: someone who helps teach a course and answer students’ questions.
glossary.software architecture: How a software system’s parts are organized so the whole thing works and stays manageable.
glossary.accidental complexity: Extra difficulty caused by tools or choices around a solution, rather than by the problem itself.
glossary.vibe coding: Making software by telling an AI what you want and letting it write the code, often without closely checking how it works.
glossary.compiler: A tool that turns code you write into a program a computer can run.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.ADHD: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a condition that can affect attention, activity, and impulse control.
glossary.circadian rhythm: The body's repeating daily timing pattern, which helps set when you feel sleepy or alert.
glossary.chronotype: Whether someone tends to be more of a morning person or an evening person.
glossary.DLMO: Dim-light melatonin onset: a point when melatonin can be measured in dim light, used to estimate someone's body-clock timing.
glossary.chronotherapy: Treatment planned around changing the timing of the body's daily clock, such as shifting sleep earlier.
glossary.bright light therapy: Using strong light at a planned time to help shift sleep and body-clock timing.
glossary.VPS: Virtual Private Server: a computer you rent and leave online to run your own software.
glossary.VPN: Virtual private network: a service that sends your internet traffic through another computer, often to protect it or make it appear to come from somewhere else.
glossary.git: A tool that keeps a history of changes to code or other files.
glossary.Yggdrasil: Network software that lets computers connect through a shared private network.
glossary.self-hosting: Running a model on computers you control instead of using someone else's online service.
glossary.20% time: A work setup where someone can use part of their job time to try a side project.
glossary.leaderboard: A ranked list showing who is ahead or most popular.
glossary.C# and .NET: C# is a language for writing software, and .NET is a set of tools that software can use to run.
glossary.ATProto: Authenticated Transfer Protocol: a set of rules that lets different social apps work with the same posts and accounts.
glossary.IRC: Internet Relay Chat: a way to chat live with people in online rooms.
glossary.JS-less: A webpage that works without JavaScript, code many sites use for interactive features.
glossary.bot-farming: Using lots of automated accounts to make something look more popular than it is.
glossary.royalties: Money paid to someone when their work is used or played.
glossary.wire fraud: A crime involving phone or internet communications used to cheat people or organizations.
glossary.dark patterns: Design tricks that push people into doing something online they might not have chosen.
glossary.royalty pool: A shared pot of royalty money that gets paid out to artists.
glossary.data lake: A place to keep data files together so different tools can use them.
glossary.Lakehouse: A setup that combines a shared collection of data files with ways to manage and query them like a database.
glossary.catalog database: A database that keeps track of what data exists and where it is.
glossary.Parquet: A file format that stores table data grouped by columns, so tools can read the columns they need.
glossary.SQL: A language people use to ask a database for information.
glossary.DataFusion: A software project that provides tools for querying and working with data.
glossary.memory safe: Designed to prevent bugs that can happen when a program uses computer memory incorrectly.
glossary.demoscene: A community where people make computer demos to show off skill and creativity.
glossary.x86 emulator: Software that imitates an x86 computer so programs made for it can run elsewhere.
glossary.WebAssembly: A way to run compiled programs inside a web browser.
glossary.VGA: Video Graphics Array: a standard for displaying graphics on a PC.
glossary.interrupt: A signal that makes a computer pause its current work to handle something.
glossary.port access: A program communicating with a piece of computer hardware.
glossary.cycle-accurate emulation: An imitation of an old computer that keeps its operations timed to match the original.
glossary.assembly: A way to write computer instructions close to the commands the machine carries out.
glossary.LED filament: A thin, bendable line of light made with LEDs.
glossary.EL wire: Electroluminescent wire: a flexible cord that glows when powered.
